newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Air NZ says more pacts to follow United.
newsitem.headline: Air NZ says more pacts to follow United.

text.p: Air New Zealand said on Tuesday it had signed a commercial alliance with the world's largest airline, United Airlines, and aimed for more pacts with other partners.
The New Zealand carrier, which owns half of Ansett Australia, said further alliances could be expected, probably with a European and an Asian carrier.
"We have said we are not stopping with just this one," Managing Director Jim McCrea told a news conference.
McCrea said the deal could help reverse the recent trend of falling passenger numbers between New Zealand and the United States, and to a lesser extent between Australia and the States.
"We think this is a significant breakthrough in increasing travel from the U.S."
He said Air New Zealand had been frustrated in getting access to the United States, but with United flying to 251 cities there,that problem should be overcome.
"We are absolutely confident that this commercial alliance with United will now allow us to focus more on outbound travel from the U.S.," he said.

Under the alliance agreement, which takes effect from March, the two airlines will continue to operate current levels of aircraft capacity on routes they both fly within the Pacific region, and will develop arrangements to share their carrying capacity and other infrastructure.
McCrea said United's frequent flier programme, with its 18 million members, would be of "huge benefit" to Air New Zealand.
The deal did not affect Ansett Holdings, in which Air New Zealand has a half share, and its own relationship with United.
While the agreement would supercede Air New Zealand's existing agreement with Delta Air Lines Inc, McCrea hoped there were areas both companies could continue to cooperate in.
He did not not see the deal as a precursor to an equity alliance with United.

The arrangement would significantly increase the number of trans-Pacific flights that each airline could offer its customers, and the number of city-to-city connections that the two airlines can provide between the United States and New Zealand or Australia.
McCrea said the economies of both Australia and New Zealand stood to make significant gains from the deal.

"It marks a real breakthrough in terms of our ability to develop the vital North American tourism market, and to extend and improve the services we can offer Australia and New Zealand travellers to the United States and beyond," McCrea said.
McCrea said United's experience with its code share alliance with Deutsche Lufthansa AG had shown such arrangements could enhance profitability.
